# Chapter 2 — OrgTree — The Governed Definition of Organizational Structure

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
What OrgTree *is* — a governed artifact, not a directory or database — its
internal structure of nodes (stable identifiers, names, types, parent
references, governance metadata), how a node's path from the root bridges to
OrgPath, how it is governed as a version-controlled artifact, and what it is
deliberately *not* responsible for.
:::

## What OrgTree Is

OrgTree is not a directory. It is not a database. It is not a tree data structure in the computer science sense, although it describes a tree in the organizational sense — a rooted hierarchy in which every node except the root has exactly one parent, and every node may have zero or more children. OrgTree is a governed artifact: a versioned, machine-readable record that defines the complete hierarchy of an organization, encompassing its divisions, departments, units, teams, functions, regions, sites, and any other segment type that the organization uses to describe its own structure. OrgTree is the authoritative answer to the question: what does this organization actually look like, expressed in terms that a computer can reason about?

The significance of framing OrgTree as an artifact — rather than as a system, a service, or a feature — is deliberate and important. An artifact is something that is authored, approved, committed, and versioned. It has a history. It can be read by a human or parsed by a machine. It can be reviewed before it is changed and audited after a change is made. Systems can be configured in inconsistent ways; services can drift from their intended state; features can be enabled or disabled without a record. An artifact, maintained under governance discipline, is the same document it was when it was last approved — or, if it has changed, the change is recorded in the commit history along with the reason for the change and the identity of the person who approved it. This is the property that makes OrgTree useful as the foundation of a governance substrate: its authority derives not from any platform's enforcement mechanism but from the discipline with which it is maintained and the pipeline that derives operational values from it.

## The Internal Structure of OrgTree

OrgTree consists of nodes and relationships. Each node represents one organizational segment — one named unit of the hierarchy. A node carries several properties, each of which serves a specific governance function. The identifier of a node is unique within the tree and is stable across renames: when a node's human-readable name changes, its identifier does not, ensuring that OrgPath values derived from a node identifier remain valid across renaming events without requiring mass re-derivation. The human-readable name of the node is the label that appears in reports, audit logs, and administrative interfaces. The type of the node indicates what kind of organizational segment it represents — division, department, unit, team, site, function, or any other category the organization recognizes — and the set of valid types is itself a governed artifact, defined once and extended deliberately. The parent reference of the node establishes its position in the tree: it names the identifier of the node directly above it in the hierarchy, and it is this reference that, taken together with the parent references of all ancestor nodes, defines the complete lineage of the node from the root of the tree.

In addition to its structural properties, each node carries governance metadata. The effective date records when the node was added to the tree or when its current form became authoritative. The review status records whether the node has been validated in the most recent governance review cycle — a mechanism for ensuring that nodes are not allowed to persist indefinitely without human confirmation that they still correspond to real organizational structure. The responsible role identifies the function or position within the organization that is accountable for the accuracy of the node, providing a clear point of contact for any governance question about that segment of the hierarchy. The root node of OrgTree represents the organization as a whole. Every other node is a descendant of the root, connected through the chain of parent references that constitutes the tree.

## Path Encoding and the Bridge to OrgPath

Because OrgTree is a tree, any node can be addressed by its path from the root — the ordered sequence of node identifiers from the root down through each successive ancestor to the node itself. This path is the organizational lineage of the node: it encodes not merely where the node is in the current state of the tree but how it is reached — through which organizational layers it passes on the way from the top of the organization to its specific position. The path of a node belonging to the Regional West unit, which is a child of Field Services, which is a child of Operations, which is a direct child of the organizational root, is the concatenated sequence of identifiers for those four nodes, ordered from outermost to innermost. This path encoding is the bridge between OrgTree and OrgPath, and it is what makes the combination of the two constructs architecturally powerful: OrgTree defines the set of valid paths, OrgPath carries the specific path for each managed asset, and the validity of any OrgPath value can be checked mechanically against the current state of the OrgTree registry.

## How OrgTree Is Governed

OrgTree is maintained as a version-controlled artifact committed to a governed repository. Every change to OrgTree — adding a node, removing a node, renaming a node's human-readable label, moving a node to a different parent, archiving a node that represents a dissolved organizational unit — is treated as a formal change event. Changes are proposed as change requests through a defined workflow, reviewed against the organization's governance process, approved by the appropriate authority, and committed to the repository with a descriptive record that captures the reason for the change, the identity of the approver, the effective date, and the downstream impact on OrgPath values and dynamic group membership rules. The commit message is not optional administrative commentary; it is the formal record of an organizational structural decision.

This governance process ensures that OrgTree reflects deliberate organizational decisions, not ad-hoc administrative actions. The version history of OrgTree is, in a meaningful sense, the history of the organization's structure — a chronological record of how the organization changed over time, available for audit, for compliance review, and for incident investigation. When a security event is investigated and the question arises of what organizational unit a particular user or device belonged to at the time of the event, the answer is available by checking the state of the OrgTree registry at the relevant date. This is not a forensic reconstruction; it is the direct consequence of treating organizational structure as a versioned artifact rather than as a mutable configuration state.

## What OrgTree Is Not Responsible For

OrgTree defines organizational structure — it does not enforce it. This is a boundary that must be clearly understood, because the value of OrgTree depends on it being kept clean. OrgTree specifies what organizational nodes exist and how they relate to one another. It does not apply policies, assign permissions, provision identities, or configure devices. Those operations are the responsibility of the governance pipeline that consumes OrgTree — the tooling that reads the registry, derives OrgPath values for each identity, and propagates those values to the management surfaces that need them. OrgTree provides the authoritative record of what is true. The pipeline is the mechanism by which that truth is expressed in the live environment. Conflating the two — expecting OrgTree itself to enforce governance rather than to define it — would be a category error, and one that would undermine the clean separation of concerns on which the architecture depends.

::: {.callout-note title="Requirement Addressed — Authoritative Registry"}
The companion document required that the organizational hierarchy itself be a governed artifact: versioned, machine-readable, and authoritative over every attribute value derived from it. OrgTree is that artifact. It is the single governed record that defines what valid organizational positions exist, what the relationships between them are, and what change history exists for every structural decision the organization has made. No other source of organizational truth competes with it. Every OrgPath value, every dynamic group membership rule, and every drift detection result is derived from OrgTree and is only valid in relation to it.
:::
